The early life stages of Saithe (Pollachius virens) begin with the release of pelagic eggs during a broadcast spawning event. Newly fertilised oocytes are transparent and measure approximately 1.15 mm in diameter, developing within the water column. Upon completion of incubation, larval eclosion occurs after approximately 9 days [ab = approximately 9 days] when water temperatures reach 9.4 °C [T = 9.4 °C]. The resulting yolk-sac larvae, or prolarvae, are lecithotrophic and carry an endogenous supply of nutrients. At the moment of chorion rupture, these newly emerged individuals possess a wet weight of about 0.0009 grams [Wwb = about 0.0009 grams], reflecting the modest size of the yolk supply. This initial mass is extremely low compared to the ultimate adult body size. The prolarvae remain non-feeding for a brief period, relying entirely on the absorbed yolk reserves until the mouth opens and retinal differentiation permits the onset of exogenous feeding, marking a critical trophic transition in the life cycle.

Juvenile and early adult growth in Saithe proceeds rapidly, with individuals attaining a relatively large body size. Field surveys and otolith-based back-calculations indicate that female fish reach sexual maturity at a total length of approximately 39.1 centimeters [Lp = approximately 39.1 centimeters], a metric commonly used to define the length at puberty for this commercially important gadoid. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for a female of this length, derived from length-weight regressions, is on the order of 543 grams [Wwp = 543 grams]. This body mass reflects the considerable somatic investment required before the onset of gonadal recrudescence. For juveniles inhabiting cooler North Atlantic waters, the onset of vitellogenesis is delayed until energetic reserves are sufficient to support the high metabolic demands of gamete production. Ultimately, the largest documented individuals reach an asymptotic or ultimate total length of 130 centimeters [Li = 130 centimeters], with the heaviest females attaining an ultimate wet weight of approximately 32,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 32,000 grams].

Under the stable thermal regime of 6 °C [T = 6 °C] that characterises much of the species' subarctic feeding grounds, key life-history transitions have been quantified. The first successful spawning event in female Saithe occurs after approximately 1,460 days after hatching [tR = approximately 1,460 days after hatching], representing a relatively protracted juvenile period that is typical of large-bodied, itero at a temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C]parous gadoids. At this same thermal regime, the maximum recorded longevity or lifespan of the species has been documented at roughly 9,125 days [am = roughly 9,125 days], equivalent to about at a temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C]25 years. This long lifespan allows individuals to participate in multiple annual spawning aggregations over several decades. The consistency of these thermal conditions in the deeper, colder portions of the species' range is thought to slow metabolic rates, thereby extending the period of somatic growth and delaying reproductive senescence until very late in life.

Reproductive output in Saithe is substantial, reflecting the species' high fecundity as a batch-spawner. At a body size of approximately 75 centimeters in total length, corresponding to a wet body mass of about 3.2 kilograms, a mature female produces an average of 2,600,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 2,600,000 eggs per spawning event] and releases them over multiple batches throughout a single spawning season each year [F_R_i = single spawning season each year] when maintained at a water temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C]. This annual fecundity places Saithe among the more prolific members of the Gadidae. The eggs are pelagic and are released in a strategy that increases the probability of larval survival by staggering emergence with pulsed planktonic productivity. The energetic cost of such high reproductive investment is considerable, requiring females to accumulate substantial lipid reserves during the preceding foraging season to fuel the vitellogenic cycle.

Comparative physiological studies highlight the remarkable scope for growth in this species. The yolk-sac larva, weighing less than one milligram at 0.0009 grams [Wwb = 0.0009 grams], undergoes a staggering increase in mass by the time it reaches the maximum adult size of 32,000 grams [Wwi = 32,000 grams], representing a gain of over seven orders of magnitude. This trajectory is supported by a piscivorous diet and efficient food conversion rates. Interestingly, although the typical lifespan under the cool 6 °C [T = 6 °C] regime of the Norwegian Sea is about 9,125 days [am = about 9,125 days], populations in more southerly, warmer waters may exhibit reduced longevity and faster maturation. The age at first reproduction, at roughly 1,460 days after hatching [tR = roughly 1,460 days after hatching] at 6 °C [T = 6 °C], is similarly influenced by thermal conditions; at the slightly warmer temperature of 9.4 °C [T = 9.4 °C], the incubation period is shortened to about 9 days [ab = about 9 days], demonstrating the strong temperature-dependence of early developmental rates in this boreal gadoid.
